## Welcome!

This newsletter isn't an official Church Army publication and as such it doesn't represent the views of Church Army. Just me, Data Dave.

## The big idea: Saying 'Yes And' to our funders {#sec-big-idea}

I had a really exciting conversation an the Mission Support Team day on Tuesday. I was talking to someone who manages a project, and they were telling me that the project stakeholders were asking the wrong questions (or at least, they weren't always asking *all the right questions*).

![](images/clipboard-4033239090.png "Arrested Development is a great show you should watch it"){fig-alt="Arrested Development's Michael Bluth saying 'Hey, that's the name of the newsletter'"}

I was absolutely thrilled, and it helped me to put my finger on something that had been bothering me: Very often there is little-to-no critical engagement with stakeholder requirements for the quantitative reporting around a project. The stakeholder says, "Please measure X" and we say, "Okay we'll ask our data guy to make it happen."

At one level, that's totally understandable: Oftentimes our stakeholders are really invested in one Big Number, and getting their money means promising to make the Big Number go up. It's beyond the scope of this newsletter to evaluate whether that's a good way of managing projects at a national level. That's simply the funding environment we're living in, which means that when a funder says, "Please measure X", we probably don't want to say "No, sorry."

But we can say, "*Yes, and...*"

> *Yes*, we can measure the number of new disciples, *and* we can measure the number of young people who say that have more joy and/or peace because of Jesus

> *Yes*, we can measure self-reported confidence in evangelism, *and* we can ask participants if they have become more imaginative, hopeful or prayerful in their evangelism.

Whatever the benefits of having a Big Number may be, there are certainly pitfalls. In my experience, people are often cynical about the realisation of targets which appear to have been 'pulled out of thin air'. At worst, quantitative impact reporting can become something of a box-ticking exercise - a necessary evil about which nobody is particularly excited. In that context, saying "*Yes, and..."* can communicate a number of important things:

1.  It communicates that we are sincerely invested in the aims of the project. We really do want new disciples and confident evangelists! Asking better questions and sharing richer data shows that we desire to understand and celebrate the reality represented by the Big Number, rather than the number for its own sake.
2.  It demonstrates our expertise. When we tell stakeholders what we would like to measure, we show them that we understand our work and the value that it adds, and that we can not only deliver the projects objectives but also help them to understand the project's impact more deeply.
3.  It builds understanding and trust. And whatever happens to the Big Number, it's often the things we can't measure - things like understanding and trust - that really get things done.

## Something I'm proud of: Customised QR-codes on address labels! {#sec-achievement}

Last month this section was all a mistake I'd learned from. This week it's about something cool I've achieved! It's my newsletter and I'll do what I like.

This is the cool thing I have done:

![It's QR codes!](/2026/images/qr-codes.jpg){fig-alt="QR codes printed on Avery postage labels. One of them has been stuck to a mug."}

More specifically, it's customised QR codes printed onto postage labels. This opens up some really cool possibilities for data collection using physical media, because it lets us attach metadata to a survey link and then physically stick it onto the corresponding piece of paper. That means you can do things like:

-   Pre-populate a survey with someone's contact details, saving them time.

-   Group learners and facilitators into cohorts when they give feedback on a physical training resource.

-   Automatically collect data on where responses have come from, even when using physical resources.

Another really nice feature of this approach is its flexibility - you can include a generic QR code in your printed resource, then use customised labels to add data to the URL on a case-by-case basis. The only real limitation is your capacity to stick labels on to things.

I've used postage-sized labels here, but this works with labels of any size. Let me know if you think it could be useful for any of your projects!

You can view the code [here](https://github.com/Church-Army/QR-codes/blob/master/qr_codes.qmd) if you're really interested.

## The lesson: Alex Dobson has Psychic Powers {#sec-lesson}

```{r psychic_powers}
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)

set.seed(pi)

# prob_nothing + prob_exact + prob_just_suit + prob_just_rank

prob_exact <- 1/52
prob_just_suit <- 1/4
prob_just_rank <- 1/13
prob_nothing <- 1 - prob_exact - prob_just_suit - prob_just_rank

points_exact <- 1/prob_exact
points_just_suit <- 1/prob_just_suit
points_just_rank <- 1/prob_just_rank
points_nothing <- 0

# flip_a_card
flip_cards <- function(n_cards, n_tests, psychic_power = 0) {
  
  rolls <- runif(n_cards * n_tests)
  
  prob_exact_psychic <- min(1/52 + psychic_power^2, 1)
  prob_just_suit_psychic <- min(1/4 + psychic_power - prob_exact_psychic, 1)
  prob_just_rank_psychic <- min(1/13 + psychic_power - prob_exact_psychic, 1)
  prob_nothing_psychic <- min(1 - prob_exact_psychic - prob_just_suit_psychic - prob_just_rank_psychic, 1)

  values <- c(
    points_nothing,
    points_just_suit,
    points_just_rank,
    points_exact
  )
  
  breaks <- cumsum(c(
    prob_nothing_psychic,
    prob_just_suit_psychic,
    prob_just_rank_psychic,
    prob_exact_psychic
  ))

  points <- matrix(
    values[findInterval(rolls, breaks) + 1L],
    nrow = n_cards)

  colSums(points)
}

scores <- flip_cards(n_cards = 10, n_tests = 1e5)
slightly_psychic_scores <- flip_cards(10, 1e5, 0.1)
highly_psychic_scores <- flip_cards(n_cards = 10, n_tests = 1e5, psychic_power = 0.4)

psychic_simulations_plot <- 
  ggplot(tibble(x = scores), aes(x = x)) +
  
  geom_density(trim = TRUE, colour = "black") +

  
  geom_density(data = tibble(x = slightly_psychic_scores), trim = TRUE,
               colour = "blue", fill = "blue", alpha = .05) + 

  
  geom_density(data = tibble(x = highly_psychic_scores), trim = TRUE,
               colour = "purple", fill = "purple", alpha = .05) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, 52)) +
  
  labs(x = "Success score", y = "Probablility density",
       title = "Probable success score by psychic ability",
       subtitle = "100,000 simulations")

psychic_annotations <- 
  annotate("text", x = 32, y = 0.03, label = "No psychich ability", hjust = "left") +
  annotate("text", x = 51, y = 0.018, label = "Psychic score: 0.1",
           colour = "blue", hjust = "left") +
  annotate("text", x = 220, y = 0.0045, label = "Psychic score: 0.4",
           colour = "purple", hjust = "left") +
  
  

psychic_simulations_plot
```

```{r bayesian_stuff}
psychic_scores <- readRDS(here("2026", "data", "psychic-testing_2026.rds"))
psychic_scores <- 
  mutate(
    psychic_scores, 
    rank_correct = rank_correct & !suit_and_rank_correct,
    suit_correct = suit_correct & !suit_and_rank_correct
  ) |> 
  rename(just_suit_correct = suit_correct, 
         just_rank_correct = rank_correct)

psychic_scores <- 
  mutate(psychic_scores, 
         just_rank_correct = just_rank_correct * points_just_rank,
         just_suit_correct = just_suit_correct * points_just_suit,
         suit_and_rank_correct = suit_and_rank_correct * points_exact)

psychic_scores <- 
  mutate(psychic_scores,
         score = just_rank_correct + just_suit_correct + suit_and_rank_correct,
         .keep = "unused")

psychic_scores <- summarise(psychic_scores, score = sum(score), .by = name)

layers <- names(psychic_simulations_plot$layers)
annotate_layers <- layers[str_detect(layers, "annotate")]

psychic_simulations_plot[[-annotate_layers]] +
  geom_vline(data = psychic_scores, aes(xintercept =  score),  colour = "orange", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(NA, 100))
```
